2790:
Chlorpromazine is a prescription medication used primarily to treat serious mental illnesses — especially schizophrenia — by calming abnormal brain activity. It was the world's very first antipsychotic drug, discovered in 1952, and its arrival completely changed how psychiatry worked. Before it existed, people with severe mental illness were subjected to treatments like physical restraints, lobotomies (surgical destruction of parts of the brain), and insulin shock therapy. Chlorpromazine replaced all of that with a pill, and in doing so, it launched an entirely new field of medicine called psychopharmacology — the science of treating mental illness with drugs.

It belongs to a class of drugs called phenothiazines, and to a broader category called first-generation (typical) antipsychotics, also historically called "major tranquilizers" or "neuroleptics." Today it remains on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines, meaning the WHO considers it one of the most important drugs that any healthcare system in the world must have access to.
How It Works — Understanding the Brain First

To understand chlorpromazine, you need a basic picture of what's happening in the brain.

Your brain communicates through chemical messengers called neurotransmitters. One of the most important ones is dopamine. Think of dopamine as a text message, and the brain cells that receive it as having a special inbox called a receptor. When dopamine docks into a receptor (specifically a type called the D2 receptor), it delivers its message and triggers a response in the brain. Dopamine is involved in movement, motivation, pleasure, emotional responses, and thinking.

In conditions like schizophrenia, certain dopamine pathways in the brain become overactive. This flooding of dopamine signals is strongly linked to positive symptoms — a medical term for things that are added to the person's experience that shouldn't be there — such as:

  • Hallucinations: Hearing voices, seeing things, or sensing things that don't exist in reality.
  • Delusions: Holding unshakeable false beliefs, like believing you're being spied on or that you have a special divine mission.
  • Disorganized thinking: Being unable to think clearly or communicate coherently.

Chlorpromazine works by blocking D2 dopamine receptors. Using the analogy from before: if dopamine is a text message and the receptor is the inbox, chlorpromazine essentially locks the inbox shut. Dopamine can no longer deliver its message, so the overactive signaling that drives psychotic symptoms gets quieted down.

However, chlorpromazine doesn't just block dopamine. It also blocks several other types of receptors throughout the brain and body, which is why it has both a wide range of uses and a wide range of side effects. Pharmacologists sometimes call it a "dirty drug" — not as an insult, but as a technical term meaning it acts on many targets at once rather than one specific one. Specifically, it also blocks:

  • Histamine H1 receptors — causing sedation and drowsiness.
  • Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors — causing blood pressure to drop.
  • Muscarinic (acetylcholine) receptors — causing dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and difficulty urinating.
  • Serotonin receptors — contributing further to its calming and antipsychotic effects.
What It Is Used To Treat

1. Schizophrenia
This is its main use. Chlorpromazine effectively reduces hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking. It is less effective for the so-called negative symptoms of schizophrenia — things that are taken away from the person, like emotional flatness, lack of motivation, and social withdrawal.

2. Bipolar Disorder (Manic Episodes)
During the manic phase of bipolar disorder, a person may feel euphoric, need almost no sleep, make impulsive decisions, and become aggressive or dangerous. Chlorpromazine can help bring this extreme state under control.

3. Severe Nausea and Vomiting
There is a specific region in the brain called the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) that acts as a vomiting control center. It has lots of dopamine receptors. By blocking those receptors, chlorpromazine is very effective at stopping severe nausea and vomiting — including that caused by cancer chemotherapy or radiation.

4. Intractable Hiccups
This is surprisingly one of chlorpromazine's most specific uses. It is actually the only drug formally approved by the FDA for persistent or intractable hiccups — meaning hiccups that last more than 48 hours and won't respond to simple remedies. The exact mechanism isn't fully understood, but its blockade of dopamine and other receptors seems to disrupt the reflex arc that causes hiccuping.

5. Severe Agitation
Chlorpromazine can rapidly calm a person who is severely agitated, combative, or in a psychiatric emergency — including those with dementia, substance-induced psychosis, or other acute crises.

6. Tetanus (as a supportive treatment)
Tetanus is a bacterial infection that causes severe, painful, uncontrollable muscle spasms. Chlorpromazine can be used alongside other treatments to help reduce those spasms.

7. Pre-Surgical Use
It has historically been used before surgery to reduce anxiety and prevent nausea.

This is where chlorpromazine gets complicated — and it's the main reason that newer antipsychotic drugs were developed. Because chlorpromazine blocks so many receptor types, it causes a wide variety of side effects.

Movement-Related Side Effects (Extrapyramidal Symptoms or EPS)

Dopamine doesn't just affect thinking — it is also critical for controlling smooth, coordinated movement. A brain region called the basal ganglia relies on dopamine to coordinate movement. When chlorpromazine blocks dopamine receptors there, it disrupts movement control. This produces a group of side effects called extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS):

  • Drug-induced Parkinsonism: Tremors (shaking), muscle rigidity, shuffling gait, and slow movement — symptoms that look identical to Parkinson's disease, though they are caused by the drug, not the disease itself.
  • Akathisia: A deeply distressing feeling of inner restlessness. The person cannot sit still and feels an almost unbearable urge to constantly move, pace, rock, or fidget. People sometimes describe it as feeling like their skin is crawling from the inside.
  • Acute Dystonia: Sudden, sustained, involuntary muscle contractions. For example, the neck may twist painfully to one side (torticollis), the eyes may roll upward and get stuck (oculogyric crisis), or the back may arch. This is alarming and can be frightening for the patient.
  • Tardive Dyskinesia (TD): This is the most serious movement-related side effect, and it is associated with long-term use. It involves involuntary, repetitive movements — usually of the face — such as lip-smacking, tongue rolling or protrusion, chewing motions, grimacing, and sometimes writhing movements of the limbs or trunk. The troubling part is that tardive dyskinesia can become permanent even after the drug is stopped. This is why monitoring is critical with long-term use.

Hormonal Effects (Hyperprolactinemia)

Normally, dopamine acts as a natural brake on the production of a hormone called prolactin (the hormone responsible for breast milk production). When chlorpromazine blocks dopamine, it removes this brake, and prolactin levels in the blood rise abnormally. This is called hyperprolactinemia, and it can cause:

  • Breast milk production in women who are not pregnant or breastfeeding (galactorrhea)
  • Breast enlargement in both women and men (gynecomastia in men)
  • Irregular or absent menstrual periods in women
  • Reduced sexual drive and erectile dysfunction in men
  • Long-term, elevated prolactin can reduce bone density, increasing fracture risk

Cardiovascular Effects

  • Orthostatic hypotension: A sudden drop in blood pressure when the person stands up from sitting or lying down. This happens because chlorpromazine blocks alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, which normally help maintain blood pressure with changes in posture. The result is dizziness, lightheadedness, and potentially fainting. This is especially dangerous in elderly patients.
  • QT prolongation: Chlorpromazine affects the electrical signaling of the heart in a way that prolongs what's called the "QT interval" on an electrocardiogram (ECG). In rare cases, this can lead to a life-threatening abnormal heart rhythm called Torsades de Pointes.

Anticholinergic Effects

These arise from the blockade of muscarinic (acetylcholine) receptors and include:

  • Dry mouth
  • Blurred vision (difficulty focusing on nearby objects)
  • Constipation
  • Difficulty urinating (urinary retention)
  • Confusion and memory difficulties, particularly in older adults

Sedation

Blocking histamine H1 receptors in the brain causes significant drowsiness, especially at the beginning of treatment or with higher doses. While sometimes useful (for calming agitated patients), it can interfere with daily functioning.

Skin and Eye Effects

  • Photosensitivity: The skin becomes abnormally sensitive to sunlight, leading to severe and easy sunburns. Patients are advised to use strong sunscreen and cover up outdoors.
  • Skin pigmentation: Long-term use can cause a grayish-purple or slate-colored discoloration of skin exposed to the sun.
  • Eye deposits: Prolonged use can cause tiny deposits in the cornea (front of the eye) and lens, potentially affecting vision.

Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)

This is a rare but potentially fatal reaction to antipsychotic drugs. It involves four hallmark features:

  1. Extremely high fever
  2. Severe, lead-pipe muscular rigidity throughout the body
  3. Altered or fluctuating consciousness (confusion, stupor)
  4. Unstable vital signs (rapidly changing blood pressure, heart rate, breathing)

NMS is a medical emergency and requires immediate hospital care. The drug must be stopped immediately and intensive treatment begun.

Lowered Seizure Threshold

Chlorpromazine makes it easier for seizures to occur. This means people with epilepsy or any other seizure disorder need to be especially careful when using it, as it may trigger or worsen seizures.

Blood (Hematological) Effects

In rare cases, chlorpromazine can suppress the bone marrow's production of white blood cells — particularly a type called granulocytes. This condition is called agranulocytosis, and it leaves the person dangerously vulnerable to infections that the immune system would normally handle easily.

Liver Effects

Chlorpromazine can cause a type of liver problem called cholestatic jaundice, where bile flow from the liver becomes blocked. Signs include yellowing of the skin and whites of the eyes (jaundice), dark urine, pale stools, and itching. This usually appears in the first few weeks of treatment and typically resolves when the drug is stopped.

Metabolic Effects

Weight gain is common, partly due to the blockade of histamine receptors, which affects appetite regulation and energy metabolism.
Contraindications — Who Should NOT Take It

Chlorpromazine should not be used in certain situations, including:

  • People who are already in a coma or have severe central nervous system (CNS) depression (e.g., from alcohol, sedatives, or opioids), because it will dangerously worsen this state.
  • People with known bone marrow suppression (already low white blood cells).
  • People with a known allergy to chlorpromazine or other phenothiazines.
  • It must be used very cautiously — often avoided — in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis, as it significantly increases the risk of stroke and death in this population.

Chlorpromazine can be given in several forms depending on the situation:

  • Oral tablets or syrup — for ongoing, regular treatment at home.
  • Intramuscular (IM) injection — for faster action in emergencies or when the patient cannot take oral medication.
  • Intravenous (IV) infusion — in hospital settings for more immediate control.
  • Rectal suppositories — when a person cannot swallow and injection is not possible.

Chlorpromazine is a first-generation (typical) antipsychotic. The drugs that came after it — risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, clozapine, and others — are called second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics. The newer drugs were designed specifically to reduce some of the worst side effects of chlorpromazine, especially the movement disorders (EPS and tardive dyskinesia) and the hormonal effects. The newer drugs are generally preferred today in most settings, but chlorpromazine is still widely used, especially in parts of the world where access to newer and more expensive drugs is limited.

Chlorpromazine's discovery in 1952 is one of the most important moments in the history of medicine. It didn't just give doctors a new tool — it fundamentally changed society's understanding of mental illness, proving that psychiatric conditions had a biological basis in the brain and could be treated with chemistry. It helped empty overcrowded psychiatric institutions around the world, allowing many people with schizophrenia to live outside hospitals for the first time. Despite its limitations and side effects, it set the foundation for every antipsychotic drug that followed.

In short: chlorpromazine is a powerful, historically groundbreaking medication that works by quieting overactive dopamine signaling in the brain, used mainly to treat psychosis, but also nausea, intractable hiccups, and agitation — with a significant side effect profile that requires careful medical supervision.

"Chockablock" means so completely crammed or stuffed full that there is almost no empty space left. It describes something packed to its absolute limit — not just full, but bursting full, with things pressed tightly together and barely any breathing room.

Imagine a closet where someone has squeezed in so many clothes that the door barely closes. Or a bus in rush hour so jammed with passengers that no one else could possibly squeeze in. That feeling — of maximum, almost uncomfortable fullness — is exactly what chockablock captures.

Chockablock almost always appears in this structure:

[Something] is chockablock with [things].

  • The cupboard was chockablock with tins and jars.
  • The street was chockablock with people.
  • Her diary was chockablock with appointments.

You can also use it without "with" when the context makes the meaning obvious:

  • "Is there space in the car?" — "No, it's absolutely chockablock."

One important note: you will almost never see it placed before the noun it describes. You wouldn't naturally say "a chockablock room." You say "the room was chockablock." It describes a state, so it sits after the thing it's describing.

This is a crucial distinction. "Full" is mild and neutral. "Chockablock" is intense and vivid. It implies:

  • Maximum capacity — not 80% full, not even 99% full. Completely, utterly stuffed.
  • Tightness — things are pressed together, leaving no gaps.
  • A slightly overwhelming sense — there's almost too much in there.

Think of the difference like this:

—ExampleMental image
Full"The bag is full."No more room, but things sit comfortably.
Chockablock"The bag is chockablock."Things are jammed in, bulging, barely zipped shut.

Saying a bag is "full" gives you a calm picture. Saying it's "chockablock" makes you picture things wedged in tightly, bulging at the seams, barely held together. The word carries a kind of pressure and intensity that "full" simply does not.
What kinds of things can be chockablock?

This is a flexible word. It works for:

Physical places and containers

  • A market chockablock with vendors and stalls.
  • A garage chockablock with old furniture and tools.
  • A beach chockablock with tourists on a summer afternoon.

Time and schedules

  • A week chockablock with deadlines and meetings.
  • A school holiday chockablock with activities for the children.

Written or spoken content

  • A speech chockablock with statistics and data.
  • A novel chockablock with rich descriptions of landscape.

The mind

  • A head chockablock with facts the night before an exam.

The common thread across all of these is the same idea: whatever the "container" is — a room, a schedule, a speech, a mind — it is packed to its very limit.

Chockablock is an informal word. It belongs in casual conversation, personal writing, journalism, and storytelling. You would not use it in a formal report, an academic essay, a legal document, or a professional business email. In those contexts, you'd reach for words like "fully occupied," "congested," or "densely populated."

What makes chockablock special is precisely its informality — it is vivid, punchy, and a little playful. It makes your writing or speech more expressive and alive. When you say a place is "chockablock," your listener immediately feels the crowdedness in a way that "full" or even "packed" doesn't quite deliver.
How it compares to similar words

There are many near-synonyms: packed, crammed, jam-packed, stuffed, crowded, overflowing, teeming, bursting. Chockablock fits comfortably in this group, but here is how it stands apart:

  • "Crowded" most naturally refers to people. Chockablock works equally well for people, objects, or even abstract things like text or a schedule.
  • "Full" is neutral and everyday. Chockablock is vivid and turns up the intensity.
  • "Packed" and "crammed" are close cousins — arguably the nearest in meaning. Chockablock is slightly more colorful and characterful than either of them.
  • "Teeming" (e.g., teeming with fish) implies living, moving things. Chockablock has no such restriction.

Chockablock means so completely and tightly stuffed or crammed with things that there is virtually no empty space left — used informally to describe places, schedules, texts, or anything that can hold contents, and almost always followed by the word "with."
2792:
Choice refers to the act, result, or freedom of selecting one thing from two or more possibilities. It always involves picking — consciously and deliberately — from a set of available options.

Three things are almost always true when "choice" is involved:

  • There must be at least two options available.
  • The person making it must have some degree of awareness — you can't accidentally make a choice.
  • There must be some freedom to pick — if you're completely forced, it's not really a choice (more on this below).

"Choice" carries three slightly different meanings depending on context. Understanding each one clearly is important.

Sense 1 — The act of choosing

Here, "choice" refers to the process or moment of deciding — the mental act of selecting.

"Making a choice between two equally good options can be difficult."
"The choice was hers to make."
"He finally made his choice after thinking for an hour."

In this sense, you'll almost always see it paired with verbs like make, face, or have:

  • make a choice (= decide)
  • face a choice (= be in a situation requiring a decision)
  • have a choice (= have the freedom or opportunity to decide)

Sense 2 — The thing chosen (the selection itself)

Here, "choice" refers to what was picked — the result or outcome of choosing.

"The red car was her choice." (= that is what she picked)
"His choice of words surprised everyone." (= the words he decided to use)
"Chocolate ice cream? That's a good choice." (= a good thing to pick)

You can evaluate the quality of a choice:

  • a wise/good/smart choice
  • a poor/bad/wrong choice
  • a bold/surprising/unexpected choice

Sense 3 — The range of options available

Here, "choice" refers to the variety or set of things you can pick from — not the act of picking, but the availability of things to pick.

"This shop has a wide choice of shoes." (= many different shoes to pick from)
"There isn't much choice when it comes to vegetarian food here." (= not many options)
"You have a choice of three colors." (= three options are available to you)

This sense is often uncountable (no "a" or plural):

  • a wide choice of... ✓
  • not much choice ✓
  • limited choice ✓
The Freedom Dimension — "Having" vs. "Not Having" a Choice

This is one of the most important things to understand about the word.

"Having a choice" means you have real freedom to decide. You are not forced. The outcome is up to you.

"You have a choice — you can stay or leave."
"It's your choice." (= the decision belongs to you; I won't decide for you)
"She went into teaching by choice." (= she chose it freely, not because she was forced)

The phrase "by choice" is very common. It means voluntarily or on purpose, not by force:

"He lives without a phone by choice."

"Having no choice" means the situation forces you — there is only one real path, or all other paths are blocked. There is no freedom.

"I had no choice but to cancel the trip." (= I was forced to cancel; there was no alternative)
"They gave me no choice." (= they removed my freedom to decide differently)
"He had little choice in the matter." (= he was mostly forced)

This is very important: saying "I have no choice" does NOT mean zero options literally exist. It means the other options are either impossible, unacceptable, or effectively unavailable — so it feels like force.
"Of One's Own Choice" — Emphasizing Voluntary Action

This phrase stresses that a decision was made freely, with no pressure:

"Nobody pushed her — it was a decision of her own choice."

This is stronger than simply saying "by choice." It emphasizes personal ownership of the decision.

These words are close in meaning but not identical. Mixing them up is a common mistake.

Choice vs. Option

  • An option is a possibility that exists — something that could be chosen.
  • A choice is what happens when you act — the decision or result of picking.
  • Think of it this way: options are the menu; choice is what you order.

"I have three options." (= three things exist that I could pick)
"I've made my choice." (= I have now selected one)

You can have options without yet making a choice. Once you pick, that pick becomes your choice.

Choice vs. Decision

  • A decision is broader. Any firm conclusion is a decision — whether it involves picking between options or not.
  • A choice specifically involves selecting from alternatives.
  • Every choice involves a decision, but not every decision is a choice.

"She decided to start a business." → a decision (broad)
"She chose marketing over finance." → a choice (selecting between options)

Choice vs. Preference

  • A preference is what you like more or favor — your personal lean.
  • A choice is what you actually select — which may or may not match your preference.
  • You can be forced to choose something that isn't your preference.

"My preference is tea, but I chose coffee because that's all there was."

Choice vs. Alternative

  • An alternative is one of two or more options, often framed as a contrast or substitute.
  • "Alternative" focuses on the fact that other options exist beside the one being considered.
  • "Choice" focuses on the act or result of picking.

"We have no alternative." (= no other option exists)
"We have no choice." (= we are forced; cannot decide freely) ← same meaning, just framed differently

"Spoilt for choice" (British English)
Having so many good options that it's hard to decide.

"There are 40 flavors — I'm absolutely spoilt for choice."

"A Hobson's choice"
Named after a real person (Thomas Hobson), this means a situation where there appears to be a choice, but really there is only one option. It's a false choice.

"It was Hobson's choice — take the job or earn nothing."

"A Sophie's choice"
A deeply painful situation where you are forced to choose between two options, both of which are terrible or involve great loss. (From the novel/film Sophie's Choice.)

"Choosing which project to cut was a real Sophie's choice."

"The choice is yours"
A phrase meaning: I am not deciding for you; you must decide.

"By choice"
Voluntarily; freely; not by force.

"Of choice"
The preferred or most commonly used option in a category.

"It became the tool of choice for designers." (= the one most designers prefer and use)

"First choice / second choice"
Ranking your preferences.

"Oxford was her first choice; Cambridge was her second choice."

Countable uses (can use a, an, or plurals):

  • "Make a choice."
  • "She had two choices."
  • "That was a difficult choice."

Uncountable uses (used without a or plural):

  • "There is little choice."
  • "Freedom of choice is important."
  • "You have no choice here."

Key prepositions with "choice":

  • choice of → the variety/range: "a choice of flavors"
  • choice between → selecting from two things: "a choice between staying and leaving"
  • choice among → selecting from more than two: "a choice among several candidates"
  • choice to + verb → the decision to do something: "the choice to remain silent"

Act of selecting"Making a choice is hard."
The thing selected"Red was her choice."
The range of options"There's a wide choice available."
Freedom to decide"It's your choice." / "I had no choice."

"Choice" is about agency, selection, and freedom. When someone has a choice, they have power. When they have no choice, that power is gone. Understanding this tension — between free choice and forced outcomes — unlocks nearly every use of this word you'll ever encounter.
2793:
A choir is an organized group of people who sing together as one unit. The key word here is organized — a choir is not just any bunch of people who happen to be singing at the same time. It is a structured group that practices regularly, learns specific pieces of music, and performs together with purpose and coordination.

Think of it this way: one singer is a soloist. Two or three singers harmonizing informally are just singers. But a trained, rehearsed group of singers — typically ten or more — performing together as a team? That is a choir.

Choirs exist in many settings:

  • Churches and places of worship — This is where the word is most classically associated. A church choir sings hymns, sacred music, and responses during religious services. They are often a central part of the worship experience.
  • Schools and universities — Most schools have a choir, which is an extracurricular or curricular group where students learn to sing together. School choirs often perform at concerts, assemblies, and competitions.
  • Concert halls and professional settings — Professional choirs perform classical choral music on stage, just as an orchestra performs instrumental music.
  • Community settings — Many towns and cities have amateur community choirs where ordinary people join simply for the love of singing together.

A choir performs choral music — music specifically written for groups of voices. This can range from ancient religious compositions (like Gregorian chant) to modern pop arrangements. Choirs perform at:

  • Religious services
  • Concerts and recitals
  • Weddings and funerals
  • Competitions and festivals
  • Television broadcasts and recordings

A choir is led by a choirmaster (also called a choral director or conductor), who stands in front of the group, directs the singing, and is responsible for training and shaping the sound of the choir.
How a Choir Is Organized — Voice Parts

One of the most important things to understand about a choir is that it is divided into voice parts, based on the natural pitch range of each singer's voice. The standard four-part choir is built around these sections:

  • Soprano — the highest female voices
  • Alto (or contralto) — the lower female voices
  • Tenor — the higher male voices
  • Bass — the lowest male voices

This four-part structure is so standard that it even has an abbreviation: SATB (Soprano, Alto, Tenor, Bass).

Each section sings a different musical line, and when all four blend together, they create harmony — that rich, full, layered sound that is the hallmark of choral music. Some choirs also include a mezzo-soprano (between soprano and alto) and a baritone (between tenor and bass).

Within each section, the singers sit or stand together and follow the same musical line. So when you look at a choir on stage, you are essentially seeing four (or more) teams of singers, each contributing a different layer to the whole sound.
A Second Meaning: The Physical Space

This is important and often surprises people. The word choir does not only refer to a group of people — it also refers to a specific area inside a church building.

In traditional church architecture, the choir (sometimes spelled quire in older texts, though "choir" is the modern standard) is the section of the church located between the main seating area (called the nave) and the altar at the far end. This is where the singers traditionally sit during services, usually in rows of carved wooden seats called choir stalls, facing each other across a central aisle.

So if someone says, "The choir was beautifully decorated," they might mean the group of singers or the architectural section of the church. Context will always tell you which meaning is intended. In most everyday usage, "choir" refers to the group of singers; the architectural meaning is more specific to discussions of church buildings.

Different kinds of choirs have specific names:

  • Chamber choir — A small choir, typically 16–40 singers, performing in intimate venues. Known for precision and detail.
  • Symphony chorus / Philharmonic choir — A large choir that performs alongside a full orchestra.
  • Gospel choir — Rooted in African-American church tradition; known for its energetic, emotional, call-and-response style of singing.
  • A cappella choir — Sings entirely without any instrumental accompaniment. "A cappella" is an Italian phrase meaning "in the chapel style."
  • Boys' choir — Made up exclusively of young boys, before their voices change. Famous examples include the Vienna Boys' Choir.
  • Mixed choir — Has both male and female singers (the most common type).
  • Male-voice choir — All male. Very traditional in countries like Wales, where male-voice choirs are a cultural institution.
  • Female choir (or treble choir) — All female or all high voices.

• Chorister — A single member of a choir. One person in the group. "She has been a chorister at the cathedral for ten years."
  • Choirmaster / Choral director — The person who trains, conducts, and leads the choir.
  • Choirboy / Choirgirl — A young boy or girl who sings in a choir, especially a church choir.
  • Choral (adjective) — Relating to a choir or choral music. "The school has an excellent choral program."
  • Chorus — A closely related word. In everyday speech, "chorus" and "choir" are often used interchangeably, but there is a subtle distinction: "choir" tends to suggest a more formal, trained group (especially in a religious or classical context), while "chorus" can be broader — it can also refer to the repeating section of a song, or a group of singers/dancers in a theatrical performance.
A Common Idiom: "Preaching to the Choir"

You will frequently encounter the phrase "preaching to the choir" (also "preaching to the converted"). This is an idiom that means you are trying to convince or persuade people who already agree with you — your effort is wasted because your audience needs no convincing.

The image behind the phrase is obvious: if you are a preacher delivering a passionate sermon about the importance of faith, but your only audience is the church choir — people who are already deeply committed believers — you are not really accomplishing much. They are already on your side.

Example: "Writing an article about climate change for an environmental magazine is preaching to the choir — the readers are already concerned about the environment."

To cement your understanding, here is how the word is naturally used:

  • "The school choir will perform at the winter concert next Friday."
  • "She has sung in the church choir every Sunday for fifteen years."
  • "The choir was divided into sopranos, altos, tenors, and basses."
  • "The cathedral's choir, with its carved wooden stalls, dates back to the fourteenth century." (architectural meaning)
  • "He was appointed choirmaster after the previous director retired."
  • "The gospel choir's powerful voices filled the entire hall."

Choir means a trained, organized group of singers who perform together. It is most strongly associated with church music but exists in schools, concert halls, and communities worldwide. The group is divided into voice parts (soprano, alto, tenor, bass) that blend into harmony. Secondarily, "choir" refers to the specific architectural section of a church where singers sit. The related adjective is choral, and a single member of a choir is called a chorister.
2794:
To choke back something means to stop a strong emotion or reaction from coming out, even though it is very difficult to do so. You feel something powerfully — like sadness, anger, or laughter — but you force yourself to hold it in and not let it show.

Think of it this way: the feeling is trying to rise up and escape, and you are pushing it back down with great effort.

This is where the phrase becomes beautifully logical once you understand it.

The word "choke" literally means to have your throat blocked so you cannot breathe properly. Now, think about what happens to your body when you are about to cry, scream, or burst out laughing — your throat tightens. There is a real, physical pressure there. Tears build up. A sob pushes against the inside of your throat. Your voice cracks.

"Choke back" captures that physical sensation. You are essentially blocking something that is rising up through your throat and forcing it back down, just like unclogging a pipe in reverse. It is a metaphor rooted in a very real bodily feeling.

The word "back" reinforces the idea of reversal — pushing something that is moving forward and outward, back inside.

This phrasal verb is almost always followed by a noun. The most common ones are:

  • Tears — She choked back tears at the funeral.
  • Sobs — He was choking back sobs as he spoke.
  • Laughter — The students choked back laughter during the boring speech.
  • Anger / rage — She choked back her anger and replied politely.
  • Grief — He choked back his grief and tried to stay strong for his children.
  • Emotion / emotions — She choked back emotion as she accepted the award.
  • A scream — He choked back a scream when he saw the injury.
  • Words — (Less common, but possible) She choked back the cruel words she wanted to say.

You will notice that all of these are strong internal reactions — things that the body or mind naturally wants to release. That is a key part of the meaning.
The Most Important Nuance: Effort and Struggle

This is what makes "choke back" different from simply "hiding" a feeling.

When you choke something back, it is not easy. The emotion is powerful, and you are visibly or internally fighting it. There is a struggle happening. Often, even though you succeed in holding the feeling in, people around you can still see the struggle — your eyes fill with water, your jaw tightens, your voice wavers, your face turns red.

So "choke back" does not mean the emotion is absent. It means the emotion is very much present, almost overwhelming you, but you are managing — just barely — to keep it from fully escaping.

This is why a sentence like "She choked back tears" feels much more powerful than "She didn't cry." The first tells you there was a battle. The second tells you almost nothing.
Grammar: How to Use It in a Sentence

"Choke back" is a transitive phrasal verb, which means it always needs an object — something being choked back. You cannot just say "She choked back" and stop there. You must say what she choked back.

Standard word order:

Subject + choke back + object

  • He choked back his rage.
  • She is choking back tears.
  • They choked back their laughter.

Can you split the phrase?
Yes, you can place the object between the verb and the particle, but this is less common and slightly awkward with longer nouns:

  • He choked his rage back. ✅ (acceptable)
  • She choked her tears back. ✅ (acceptable)

However, when using a pronoun as the object, splitting is actually the preferred structure:

  • He choked it back. ✅ (correct — pronoun must go in the middle)
  • He choked back it. ❌ (incorrect — pronouns cannot come after the particle)

Tense forms (all regular):

  • Base form: choke back
  • Third person singular: chokes back
  • Past simple: choked back
  • Past participle: choked back
  • Present participle: choking back

Reading a phrase in real sentences is the fastest way to understand it deeply. Study these carefully:

  1. When her name was called at the ceremony, she choked back tears and walked to the stage.

(She was very emotional but stopped herself from crying in public.)

  1. The soldier choked back his grief as he stood at his comrade's grave.

(The grief was overwhelming, but he forced himself to remain composed.)

  1. I had to choke back laughter when my boss mispronounced the word for the third time.

(Laughing would have been inappropriate, so I suppressed it with effort.)

  1. He choked back his anger and spoke in a calm, measured voice.

(Inside, he was furious, but he chose not to show it.)

  1. Choking back a sob, she whispered, "I miss you so much."

(Note: the participle form "choking back" is often used at the start of a sentence to describe what someone is doing while they do something else.)

  1. The little boy choked back a scream when the dog lunged at him.

(His natural reaction was to scream, but he somehow suppressed it.)
Register and Tone: When and Where Is It Used?

"Choke back" is a neutral to slightly literary phrase. This means:

  • You will hear it in everyday spoken English — in conversations, news reports, and interviews.
  • You will also read it frequently in novels, journalism, and formal writing, because it is expressive and vivid.
  • It is not slang. It is not overly formal. It sits comfortably in the middle, making it very versatile.
  • It is used across all English-speaking countries (American, British, Australian, etc.) without any regional restriction.
Similar Expressions — and How They Differ

Understanding how "choke back" compares to similar phrases sharpens your understanding of what makes it unique.

Fight back (tears/anger/emotion)
This is the closest synonym. "Fight back tears" and "choke back tears" are nearly interchangeable. However, "fight back" emphasizes the battle or struggle slightly more, while "choke back" emphasizes the physical, throat-tightening sensation more. Both suggest strong effort.

  • She fought back tears. — Focus: the battle.
  • She choked back tears. — Focus: the physical pressure of suppressing emotion.

Hold back (tears/anger)
"Hold back" is broader and more neutral. It can apply to many situations beyond emotion (e.g., "Hold back the crowd," "Hold back information"). It does not carry the same sense of physical throat-tightening that "choke back" does. "Hold back" is slightly softer and less dramatic.

Suppress
"Suppress" is more clinical and formal. It is used in psychology, medical writing, and academic contexts. It does not carry the vivid physical imagery of "choke back." You would say "suppress emotions" in a research article; you would say "choke back tears" in a novel.

Swallow (your feelings/pride/anger)
"Swallow" is also metaphorical and relates to the throat, similar to "choke back." However, "swallow your feelings" often implies a longer-term, habitual suppression rather than a specific moment of effort. It can also imply something unhealthy — bottling up emotions over time. "Choke back" is almost always about a specific, immediate moment.

It is worth being clear about what this phrase does not mean, so you never confuse it:

  • It does not mean to choke on something (like food). "He choked on his food" is a literal use of "choke" with a completely different meaning — don't mix them up.
  • It does not mean to block or stop a physical object. It is used exclusively for emotions and internal reactions.
  • It does not mean the emotion is fake or manufactured. The emotion is always real and strong — the person simply chooses not to express it outwardly.

"Choke back" = to force a strong emotion or reaction back inside, with great effort, especially one that makes your throat feel tight.

Every time you see it, picture someone standing at a moment of intense emotion — grief, rage, joy — with their throat tight and their jaw clenched, doing everything they can to stay composed. That is "choke back."
2795:
A choke hold is a grip applied around a person's neck that cuts off either their air supply, their blood supply to the brain, or both — causing them to become helpless, unconscious, or in extreme cases, to die.

Think of it this way: your neck is one of the most vulnerable parts of your body because every vital supply your brain needs — oxygen from breathing and blood carrying nutrients — passes through it. A choke hold exploits exactly this vulnerability.

Not all choke holds work the same way. There are two fundamentally different kinds:

1. The Air Choke (Tracheal Choke)

This targets the windpipe (trachea) — the tube at the front of your throat through which you breathe. Pressure is applied directly to the front of the neck, physically crushing or compressing this tube. The person can no longer breathe properly. It feels like being strangled. This type is painful, takes longer to cause unconsciousness, and is considered more dangerous and cruder.

2. The Blood Choke (Vascular Choke)

This is more sophisticated. Instead of blocking the airway, it applies pressure to the sides of the neck, squeezing the carotid arteries — the large blood vessels that carry blood (and therefore oxygen) from the heart to the brain. When blood flow is cut off, the brain is starved of oxygen almost instantly. A person can lose consciousness in as little as 3 to 5 seconds. This type doesn't cause as much pain, and when released promptly, the person usually regains consciousness on their own. It's the kind used in martial arts.

The most classic form of a choke hold involves one person approaching another from behind. The attacker or practitioner slides one arm around the other person's neck, with the crook of the elbow positioned directly under the chin or against the throat. The other hand is used to lock the grip in place — for example, by pressing the back of the opponent's head forward, increasing the pressure. This is often called a rear naked choke in martial arts.

But choke holds can also be applied from other positions — from the front, from the ground, or even using the legs (a "triangle choke" in grappling sports). The common thread in all of them is: control the neck, control the person.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

In Sports and Martial Arts

Choke holds are legal and common in combat sports like:

  • Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu (BJJ)
  • Judo
  • Mixed Martial Arts (MMA)
  • Wrestling

Here, a choke hold is used as a submission technique — you apply it until your opponent "taps out" (signals defeat) or loses consciousness. When used correctly by trained practitioners, blood chokes are considered relatively safe because the hold is released immediately.

In Law Enforcement

Police have historically used choke holds to physically restrain people who are resisting arrest. This has been deeply controversial. Because it requires precise application and can go fatally wrong very quickly, many police departments around the world have banned or severely restricted its use. The word "choke hold" frequently appears in legal, political, and human rights discussions for exactly this reason.

In Self-Defense

Choke holds are taught in many self-defense programs because they can quickly incapacitate an attacker regardless of size differences. However, they are also considered lethal-force techniques in many legal jurisdictions — meaning using one in a fight carries serious legal consequences.

"Choke hold" is very commonly used outside of physical fighting to describe any situation where one entity has such overwhelming, suffocating control over another that the other cannot move, grow, or escape freely.

Examples:

  • "The monopoly gave the corporation a choke hold on the entire industry." — meaning the company controlled the market so completely that no competitor could survive.
  • "Fear had a choke hold on his ambitions." — meaning fear was suppressing and suffocating his ability to act.
  • "The landlord's choke hold on the neighbourhood raised rents for everyone."

The logic of the metaphor is direct: just as a physical choke hold restricts a person's most basic freedom (breathing, consciousness), a figurative choke hold restricts an entity's most basic freedom (to compete, to grow, to act).
Why It Matters: The Danger Factor

The reason "choke hold" carries such weight as a word is because of how quickly and silently it can become fatal. Unlike a punch, which causes immediate visible damage, a choke hold can render someone unconscious in seconds with almost no warning signs — and if held for too long (generally beyond a couple of minutes after unconsciousness), it can cause brain damage or death due to prolonged oxygen deprivation. This is why even trained professionals are warned to treat it with extreme caution.

AspectDetail

To pull it all together in plain words: A choke hold is a grip around the neck used to cut off a person's air or blood supply, making them helpless or unconscious. It is used in martial arts as a submission technique, by law enforcement as a restraint method (controversially), and in self-defense. Figuratively, it means suffocating, total control over someone or something.
2796:
When something is described as choking, it means it is so thick, dense, strong, or overwhelming that it blocks or tightens the ability to breathe — or feels like it does. The word captures a specific kind of intensity: not just unpleasant, but physically restricting.

The key image is always the same: something squeezing or filling the throat and airway so tightly that normal breathing becomes difficult or impossible.
Sense 1: Physical — something that makes breathing hard

This is the most literal use. A smell, smoke, dust, gas, or any substance in the air can be described as "choking" when it is so thick or strong that it makes your throat tighten and your breath catch.

  • The factory released choking fumes into the air.
  • Firefighters worked through choking smoke.
  • A choking cloud of dust rose from the collapsed building.

Notice what "choking" adds that a word like "strong" or "thick" does not: it tells you the air itself is working against you, like invisible hands pressing on your throat. It is not just an inconvenience — it is an assault on your breathing.
Sense 2: Emotional — an overwhelming feeling in the throat

When emotions are so powerful that they create a physical tightening in the throat — making it hard to speak, breathe normally, or hold back tears — those emotions are described as choking.

  • A choking sob escaped her lips when she heard the news.
  • He felt a choking grief that made words impossible.
  • There was a choking tenderness in her voice as she said goodbye.

Here, the emotion is so intense it becomes almost physical — it sits in the throat like a blockage. The person is not literally unable to breathe, but the sensation is so close to it that the word "choking" is exactly right.
Sense 3: Biological/environmental — blocking and suffocating growth

In nature, plants or organisms that grow so densely that they block out light, space, or air for everything around them are called choking. They do not just compete — they suffocate.

  • Choking weeds had overrun the garden.
  • Choking vines wrapped around the old oak tree.
  • The river was clogged with choking algae.

The idea is the same: something is so thick and overwhelming that normal life around it cannot breathe or survive.
The thread that connects all three uses

Every use of "choking" as an adjective shares one essential quality: extreme, suffocating intensity. The thing described is not merely strong, heavy, or unpleasant — it actively prevents breathing, either literally or in the way it feels. That tightening of the airway is always the reference point, whether the cause is smoke, grief, or weeds.

This is also why "choking" is more vivid and dramatic than words like "thick," "strong," or "overwhelming." Those words describe degree. "Choking" describes an experience — the alarming feeling of breath being taken from you.
What choking does NOT mean in this form

It does not describe the person struggling. If someone is struggling to breathe, you would say the person is choking (verb). But when "choking" is used as an adjective before a noun, it describes the thing causing that struggle:

  • ✅ The choking smoke made everyone leave. → The smoke is being described.
  • ❌ The choking man ran outside. → This would be odd; here you would use "choking" as a verb/participle, not an adjective in the same sense.

"Choking" is never mild. A smell that is merely unpleasant is not choking. Smoke you can breathe through with minor discomfort is not choking. The word sits at the extreme end of the scale — used only when the thing described reaches the point of blocking function, not just reducing comfort. When you see "choking," expect severity.
2797: Choler has two meanings that are deeply connected to each other — one is medical (and ancient), the other is emotional. Understanding the first one makes the second one click perfectly.

For over a thousand years — from ancient Greece through the Middle Ages and into the early modern period — doctors across the world believed that the human body was governed by four fluids, called the four humors. These were blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile.

Choler was yellow bile — a sharp, bitter fluid believed to be produced by the liver and stored in the gallbladder. Each of the four humors was thought to control not just your physical health, but also your mood, personality, and mental state.

When your body had the right amount of choler, you were fine. But when you had too much of it, that excess yellow bile was believed to literally heat up your body from the inside — and this internal heat, doctors believed, would agitate your mind and make you explosive, impatient, and hot-tempered.

This medical theory, called humorism, has been completely replaced by modern science. But the emotional vocabulary it gave birth to has survived in the English language.
The Emotional Meaning: Fierce, Fiery Anger

Because excess choler was believed to cause anger, the word itself came to mean anger — specifically a hot, sharp, quick-to-ignite kind of anger. This is not quiet sadness, not slow-burning bitterness, and not cold hatred. Choler is the kind of anger that flares up fast and burns intensely — think of someone who snaps at the slightest provocation, whose temper rises like a sudden flame.

So if you read, "His choler rose at the insult," it simply means: his fierce anger was provoked by the insult. Or "She was full of choler" means she was in a state of hot, barely-controlled rage.

Choler is an archaic word — meaning it is old-fashioned and rarely appears in everyday modern speech or writing. You will encounter it most in:

  • Classic English literature, especially Shakespeare and other writers from the 1500s and 1600s. Shakespeare used it frequently to describe characters who were hot-tempered or enraged.
  • Historical writing about ancient or medieval medicine and the theory of humors.
  • Formal or literary modern writing, where a writer consciously chooses it for its old, weighty, dramatic flavor.
The Related Word You'll See More Often: Choleric

The adjective built from choler is choleric, and this one you will encounter more regularly — even in contemporary writing. It means easily angered, quick-tempered, or irritable as a personality trait.

For example: "He was a choleric man who erupted at the smallest things."

While "choler" refers to a state of anger in a moment, "choleric" typically describes a person's general disposition — their tendency to anger easily as part of their character.

Here is the cleanest way to hold all of this in your head:

Ancient medicine believed yellow bile (choler) made people angry when they had too much of it. So over time, "choler" stopped being just a medical word for a bodily fluid and became a word for the emotion that fluid was thought to produce: fierce, hot, impatient anger.

When you see "choler" in an old book, picture a person whose inner fire is burning too high — someone seething, easily provoked, on the edge of an outburst. That is choler.
2798: Cholera is a serious infectious disease that attacks a person's digestive system — specifically the small intestine — and can cause extreme, life-threatening dehydration very rapidly if not treated.
Cholera is caused by a bacterium called Vibrio cholerae. A bacterium is a tiny, single-celled living organism — far too small to see with the naked eye — that can enter your body and make you sick.

The bacteria spread almost entirely through contaminated water and food — particularly water or food that has been in contact with the feces (stool) of an infected person. This typically happens in places where:

  • Clean drinking water is not available
  • Sewage (waste water) mixes with drinking water
  • Food is prepared in unhygienic conditions

You cannot catch cholera just by being near someone who has it or by touching them casually. It has to enter through your mouth, usually via contaminated water or food. Raw or undercooked seafood — especially shellfish like oysters from polluted water — is a well-known source.

Once you swallow the bacteria, they travel to your small intestine. There, they produce a powerful toxin (a poison made by the bacteria). This toxin forces the cells lining your intestine to release enormous amounts of water and salt into your gut — far more than normal.

Your body then tries to get rid of all this fluid through severe, uncontrollable diarrhea. This diarrhea is so distinctive that doctors call it "rice-water stool" — pale, watery, and in very large volumes. Vomiting often follows as well.

The real danger isn't the bacteria itself — it's dehydration. Your body is losing fluids and essential minerals (called electrolytes, such as sodium and potassium) so fast that your blood pressure drops, your kidneys start failing, your muscles cramp painfully, and eventually your heart and other organs can fail. Without treatment, a person can go from healthy to dead within hours — sometimes as fast as 12 hours.

The main symptoms are:

  • Profuse, watery diarrhea — sudden and massive in volume
  • Vomiting
  • Muscle cramps, especially in the legs
  • Extreme thirst
  • Sunken eyes and cheeks, dry mouth — classic signs of severe dehydration
  • Rapid heart rate and low blood pressure
  • In very severe cases: sunken skin that stays "tented" when you pinch it, confusion, and unconsciousness

Importantly, many people infected with Vibrio cholerae — roughly 75 out of every 100 — never develop any symptoms at all, or have only mild ones. But they can still pass the bacteria in their stool and unknowingly contaminate water sources, spreading the disease to others.

Without treatment, cholera kills roughly 25–50% of severely ill patients. With proper, prompt treatment, that death rate drops to below 1%. So it is extremely deadly if ignored, but highly survivable if treated quickly. This is why access to healthcare in affected regions is so critical.

The treatment is surprisingly straightforward in most cases: replace the lost fluids and electrolytes. This is done through:

  • Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) — a carefully measured mixture of water, salts, and sugar, which the patient drinks. It sounds simple, but it has saved millions of lives. The ratio of salt and sugar matters because it helps the intestine absorb water even when infected.
  • Intravenous (IV) fluids — for severe cases where the patient is vomiting too much to drink, or is already in shock, fluids are given directly into the bloodstream through a needle.
  • Antibiotics — these can shorten the duration of illness and reduce the amount of bacteria shed in the stool, but they are secondary to rehydration. Rehydration is the priority.

Cholera is almost entirely preventable with:

  1. Clean, safe drinking water — treated (boiled or chlorinated) water prevents the bacteria from entering the body
  2. Good sanitation — proper sewage systems that keep human waste away from water supplies
  3. Hand hygiene — washing hands with soap and clean water, especially before eating and after using the toilet
  4. Safe food handling — cooking food properly, avoiding raw seafood from polluted waters
  5. Oral cholera vaccines — available and effective, though not 100%, they provide meaningful protection and are recommended for people traveling to or living in high-risk areas

Cholera is most common in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Haiti, where access to clean water and sanitation is limited. It thrives in crowded, disaster-stricken, or impoverished settings — places like refugee camps, areas hit by floods or earthquakes, or regions without reliable water infrastructure.

Throughout history, cholera has caused massive pandemics — worldwide outbreaks. There have been seven major cholera pandemics in recorded history, with the seventh (and ongoing) one beginning in 1961. It has killed tens of millions of people over the centuries, making it one of the most historically significant infectious diseases in human history.

Today, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates there are 1.3 to 4 million cholera cases annually worldwide, with 21,000 to 143,000 deaths per year — nearly all of which could be prevented with clean water and basic sanitation.

Cholera is a fast-moving, potentially fatal infectious disease caused by swallowing a specific bacterium through contaminated water or food. It kills primarily by rapidly draining the body of fluids. It is almost completely preventable with clean water and sanitation, and almost completely treatable with timely rehydration. It remains a major public health problem in parts of the world that lack access to these basic necessities.
2799: Choleric means having a hot, quick temper — the kind of person who gets angry fast, often over things that wouldn't bother most people, and whose anger tends to be intense and visible. If someone is choleric, they don't simmer quietly; they flare up. Think of a kettle that reaches boiling point in seconds rather than minutes.

The word describes a personality trait or a habitual way of being, not just a single moment of anger. When you call someone choleric, you are saying something about their nature — that anger is their default reaction to friction, inconvenience, or opposition.

A choleric person tends to be:

  • Easily triggered. Small provocations — a slow driver, a wrong answer, a minor mistake by someone else — can spark a strong reaction.
  • Intense in their anger. Their irritation doesn't stay mild. It tends to escalate quickly into visible rage, sharp words, raised voices, or explosive outbursts.
  • Not necessarily mean. This is an important nuance. A choleric person isn't always cruel or malicious. They may genuinely care about people. They simply have a very low boiling point and poor control over their temper.
A Spectrum: How Choleric Looks in Practice

It helps to imagine choleric on a scale:

At the milder end, a choleric person is simply irritable and short-fused — they snap at people, lose patience quickly, and get visibly frustrated when things don't go their way.

At the stronger end, a choleric person may have explosive outbursts — shouting, slamming things, saying harsh things in the heat of the moment. Their anger comes on like a storm: sudden, loud, and intense.

What stays consistent across the spectrum is that the anger comes fast and feels disproportionate to the trigger. Someone who is choleric might explode over spilled coffee or a two-minute delay in a way that a calmer person simply wouldn't.
The Historical Layer (Important for Full Understanding)

The word has a rich background in an ancient theory of human personality called the Four Temperaments, which said that every person's character was shaped by four bodily fluids (called "humors"). One of these fluids was yellow bile, and people who had too much of it were said to be "choleric."

In this old framework, the choleric temperament was defined by a specific cluster of traits: ambitious, driven, decisive, and energetic — but also quick-tempered, domineering, and impatient. This historical meaning is why choleric, even today, sometimes carries the suggestion of someone who is forceful and decisive, not just angry. A choleric leader, for instance, might be someone who gets things done with fierce energy but has a short fuse and doesn't handle disagreement well.

The other three temperaments were sanguine (cheerful, sociable), melancholic (thoughtful, sad), and phlegmatic (calm, slow to react) — and it's worth knowing that phlegmatic is essentially the opposite of choleric. A phlegmatic person is nearly unflappable; a choleric person is nearly always on the edge of flaring up.

While the theory of bodily humors is no longer taken seriously in medicine, this framework deeply influenced literature, psychology, and everyday language for centuries. Even today, calling someone choleric echoes that long history.
How the Word Is Used Today

In modern English, "choleric" is a formal and somewhat literary word. You are more likely to find it in books, essays, or careful writing than in everyday conversation. In casual speech, people would more commonly say someone is hot-tempered, short-fused, or quick to anger.

You can use it in two ways:

1. To describe a person's general personality:

"He was a choleric man who could not tolerate mistakes, however small."
"Her choleric nature made her a demanding but highly effective manager."

2. To describe a specific mood, look, or behavior in a moment:

"She shot him a choleric glare across the table."
"His choleric outburst silenced the entire room."
How It Differs From Similar Words

Many words are close to choleric in meaning, but each has a slightly different flavor:

  • Irritable — easily annoyed, but the feeling is often more of mild frustration than full anger. Less intense than choleric.
  • Irascible — very close to choleric, and nearly interchangeable. Irascible emphasizes the tendency to get angry easily and is equally formal.
  • Hot-tempered — a plain, everyday phrase for the same idea. Less vivid and literary than choleric.
  • Volatile — emphasizes unpredictability more than choleric does. A volatile person may swing between moods; choleric is more specifically about anger.
  • Cantankerous — emphasizes being grumpy, quarrelsome, and difficult to deal with. Choleric is more about explosive anger; cantankerous is more about chronic grumpiness and stubbornness.
  • Fiery — can mean passionate and energetic in a positive sense, or hot-tempered. More ambiguous than choleric.

The clearest near-synonym for choleric, in most contexts, is irascible — both describe a person who is habitually quick to anger in an intense way.
The One-Sentence Definition You Can Always Return To

If you ever need to distill this word to its essence:

Choleric means having a quick, explosive temper — the trait of a person who gets intensely angry fast and is easily set off by relatively small things.

Everything else — the historical layer, the nuance of intensity, the literary register — adds depth to that core idea.
